plain_text:
Migraine Trainer® is an app
developed by the National
Institute of Neurological
Disorders and Stroke
(NINDS) to help teens
understand possible
causes of their migraine
attacks and create an
individual migraine
management plan
with their parents and
health care providers.
semantic_text:
Migraine Trainer® is an app developed by the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke
(NINDS) to help teens understand possible causes of their migraine attacks and create an individual migraine management plan with their parents and health care providers.

plain_text:
7) Your sleep. Not getting enough sleep or sleeping too
much can be a migraine trigger. A serious medical condition
called sleep apnea is also associated with migraine.
semantic_text: 7) Your sleep. Not getting enough sleep or sleeping too much can be a migraine trigger. A serious medical condition called sleep apnea is also associated with migraine.

plain_text:
How to cope: Try to get between seven and nine hours of
sleep each night and talk to your doctor if you have concerns
about your sleep or think you might have sleep apnea.
semantic_text: How to cope: Try to get between seven and nine hours of sleep each night and talk to your doctor if you have concerns about your sleep or think you might have sleep apnea.

plain_text:
8) Your environment. Bright lights, loud noises,
and strong smells can all be triggers, and they can make
symptoms worse during an attack.
semantic_text: 8) Your environment. Bright lights, loud noises, and strong smells can all be triggers, and they can make symptoms worse during an attack.

plain_text:
How to cope: Avoid or reduce your exposure to these
triggers when you can and ask the people around you
to help. Ask your office mate to leave their perfume or
cologne at home, block bright outdoor light with dark
sunglasses, and try wearing earplugs or noise-canceling
headphones to muffle loud sounds.
semantic_text: How to cope: Avoid or reduce your exposure to these triggers when you can and ask the people around you to help. Ask your office mate to leave their perfume or cologne at home, block bright outdoor light with dark sunglasses, and try wearing earplugs or noise-canceling headphones to muffle loud sounds.

plain_text:
9) Medication overuse. Some medications, including
ones used to treat migraine, can cause or worsen migraine
symptoms if you take them too often.
semantic_text: 9) Medication overuse. Some medications, including ones used to treat migraine, can cause or worsen migraine symptoms if you take them too often.

plain_text:
How to cope: Make sure you know the recommended
dose and frequency for any medications you're taking.
If a medication you take is causing an increase in your
migraine attacks, talk with your doctor about switching to
a different drug.
semantic_text: How to cope: Make sure you know the recommended dose and frequency for any medications you're taking. If a medication you take is causing an increase in your migraine attacks, talk with your doctor about switching to a different drug.

plain_text:
10) Smoking and tobacco. The nicotine in cigarettes
and e-cigarettes constricts blood vessels in your brain
by making them narrower and tighter, which can trigger
migraine attacks.
semantic_text: 10) Smoking and tobacco. The nicotine in cigarettes and e-cigarettes constricts blood vessels in your brain by making them narrower and tighter, which can trigger migraine attacks.

plain_text:
How to cope: If you smoke or use tobacco products, make a
plan to quit. If you don't use tobacco products, it's always
a good idea to stay away from secondhand smoke.
semantic_text: How to cope: If you smoke or use tobacco products, make a plan to quit. If you don't use tobacco products, it's always a good idea to stay away from secondhand smoke.

plain_text:
There are up to four phases of a migraine attack, but
not everyone who experiences migraine goes through
all of these stages.
semantic_text: There are up to four phases of a migraine attack, but not everyone who experiences migraine goes through all of these stages.

plain_text:
This phase (also called the “premonitory
phase”) usually starts about a day before the
attack starts. During prodrome, you might
notice changes alerting you that a migraine
is coming. These changes can include:
semantic_text: This phase (also called the “premonitory phase”) usually starts about a day before the attack starts. During prodrome, you might notice changes alerting you that a migraine is coming. These changes can include:

plain_text:
■ Unexplained mood changes
■ Feeling more sensitive to light, sounds,
or smells
■ Craving certain foods
■ Yawning repeatedly
■ Increased thirst and urination
semantic_text: ■ Unexplained mood changes ■ Feeling more sensitive to light, sounds, or smells ■ Craving certain foods ■ Yawning repeatedly ■ Increased thirst and urination

plain_text:
This phase can happen just before or
during a migraine headache. Symptoms of
aura are usually visual, and you might see
flashing or bright lights or zig-zag lines.
You might also have nonvisual symptoms
like weak muscles, difficulty speaking, or
numbness in part of your body.
semantic_text: This phase can happen just before or during a migraine headache. Symptoms of aura are usually visual, and you might see flashing or bright lights or zig-zag lines. You might also have nonvisual symptoms like weak muscles, difficulty speaking, or numbness in part of your body.

plain_text:
During this phase, you might feel throbbing
or pulsing pain on one or both sides of
your head. The pain usually starts slowly
and then becomes more intense, and it
can get worse when you move, cough, or
sneeze. You might feel extra sensitive to
light, sounds, and smells. Many people feel
nauseous during this phase and sometimes
vomit. Some people have migraine attacks
without a headache but can still experience
other migraine symptoms.
semantic_text: During this phase, you might feel throbbing or pulsing pain on one or both sides of your head. The pain usually starts slowly and then becomes more intense, and it can get worse when you move, cough, or sneeze. You might feel extra sensitive to light, sounds, and smells. Many people feel nauseous during this phase and sometimes vomit. Some people have migraine attacks without a headache but can still experience other migraine symptoms.

plain_text:
This phase (sometimes called a "migraine
hangover") comes after the headache
and can last for a day or two. You may feel
drained, weak, and confused, and you might
also have some lingering migraine symptoms.
semantic_text: This phase (sometimes called a "migraine hangover") comes after the headache and can last for a day or two. You may feel drained, weak, and confused, and you might also have some lingering migraine symptoms.
